acts.sum: Choose a video that matters to your own research interest and turn it into a teaching object. First watch it and decide, yourself, the three or four moments where a viewer's understanding could fail. Then ask an approved tool to draft candidate questions for those moments. Treat every draft as a candidate only: keep the ones that probe the failure you identified, rewrite the ones that test recall when you wanted reasoning, and discard the rest. acts.sum: When you want to know how a teaching change landed, stop asking people to rate it. Interview a handful of students about the method you used and collect what they say in their own words. Ask an approved tool to help you cluster those transcripts into candidate statements, then write the final set yourself, aiming for around thirty statements that between them cover the enthusiasms, the complaints and the indifference you actually heard. Have a colleague review the set for statements that are really two statements, or that no one could disagree with. Pilot it on two or three students for clarity before you use it. Then give each participant the statements and ask them to place each one in a forced distribution from strong disagreement to strong agreement, so that they must decide what matters most rather than agreeing with everything. The source is explicitly a conceptual pilot with no empirical validation and its full toolkit sits in supplementary material not obtained here.

Requiring the barrier to be named before the help is chosen is our addition and is the whole point: the source shows that fit between need and function is what makes a tool useful, so a student who cannot state the need cannot judge the fit. The privacy framing is also ours, and it rests on the source's finding that 94 percent of respondents feared being accused of misconduct for using support. acts.na: Take the same written description to a writing center, a tutor, or your institution's disability service and ask what support exists for that specific step. The description is the activity; where you take it is the variable.
rel: Exploring the affordances of generative AI in academic writing for students with disabilities: A bottom-up approach to inform GenAI policies
acts.sum: Before choosing any tool for a piece of writing, describe in your own words what is actually hard about it for you. Be specific about the step rather than the task: is it that the reading is too long to hold, that the terminology will not resolve, that the ideas are there but come out in the wrong order, that the first sentence will not come, or that the whole thing is too big to start? Write it down. Then, and only then, decide what would help, and check whether the help you are considering addresses the step you named or a different one. If you cannot name the step, that is the finding, and it is worth taking to a tutor or a writing adviser rather than to a tool. Keep the description; the same barrier usually recurs and you will stop rediscovering it. This is your working document. Nobody else needs to see it and you do not need to explain to anyone why you made it.
acts.t: Name the Barrier Before You Name a Tool

The draft-first sequence, the surface-only scope, the change-by-change acceptance and the retained original are all our additions, and they exist to answer the source's third affordance gap: 69 percent of respondents feared their own voice would be overshadowed by a system they perceived as more intelligent than themselves. Writing first is the structural answer to that fear rather than a reassurance about it. American spelling normalized in editorial text (explicit word list; source wording untouched).

acts.gate: The student generates the paragraph's thinking before any process touches it, and decides change by change which corrections cross from surface into meaning.
acts.na: Use a proofreading service, a writing center appointment, or a reader you trust, with the same instruction to correct surface and leave the argument alone. Keep the original draft identically.
rel: Exploring the affordances of generative AI in academic writing for students with disabilities: A bottom-up approach to inform GenAI policies
acts.sum: Write the paragraph before you ask anything of a tool, and write it badly if that is what it takes to get it out. Accept that the spelling will be wrong, the grammar uneven, the sentences longer than they should be. The point is that the thinking is yours and exists on the page before any other process touches it. Then, if you use a tool to proofread, scope the request tightly: ask it to correct spelling, grammar and word choice, and to leave the argument alone. Read every change it proposes and accept each one individually rather than taking the result whole. Where a correction alters what you meant rather than how you said it, reject it and keep your version, even if yours reads worse. Keep the original draft. If anyone asks whether the work is yours, the original is your answer, and having it is worth more than the time it costs.
acts.t: Write It Badly First, Then Ask Only About the Surface

acts.chg: Orientation and structuration are the source's two plannability sub-affordances, reported by 10 and 14 percent of respondents respectively. The blank page is the source's own example: a respondent describes asking for a starting sentence specifically so as not to stare at a blank page with nothing on it, and others describe breaking essays into smaller tasks to avoid fatigue and maintain a routine. The source treats this as a straightforward benefit and reports that reducing anxiety around starting allows students to approach study with more confidence. Our addition is the requirement to produce your own sentence and ordering first and to request an alternative rather than an origin. That addition is not in the source and it may cost something the source values, since a respondent who cannot start at all is not helped by being told to start. Faculty should treat it as adjustable rather than fixed.

acts.gate: The student generates their own first sentence and the next three steps before any ordering is proposed, and a reason for the ordering they finally choose.
acts.na: Write the sentence and the three steps, then talk them through with a peer or a study adviser who proposes an alternative ordering. Everything else, including choosing and stating why, is unchanged.
rel: Exploring the affordances of generative AI in academic writing for students with disabilities: A bottom-up approach to inform GenAI policies
acts.sum: When a blank page is the obstacle, write your own first sentence before asking for one, and let it be a poor sentence. Write what the piece is about in the plainest terms you can manage, even if it is a sentence you know you will delete. Then break the task into the next three things you would have to do, in order, without worrying whether the order is right. If you then use a tool to help structure, give it your sentence and your three steps and ask it to propose an alternative ordering with a reason, rather than asking it where to start. Compare the two orderings and choose, and say to yourself why. The difference between these two requests is the difference between getting help with a plan you made and receiving a plan you did not. Both get you off the blank page. Only one leaves the shape of the work yours.
acts.t: Put Down Your Own Bad First Sentence

acts.chg: Focalisation is the source's fourth expressibility sub-affordance, reported by 17 respondents and valued particularly by those with neurodiversity or dyslexia who described difficulty tracking whether they were directly answering the question. The source reports that tools helped by providing targeted feedback based on rubric criteria, and its survey instrument lists validating a draft against assessment criteria as one of the ten academic writing uses respondents were asked about. The self-first sequence, the unmet-unless-located rule, the disagreement-as-question framing and the submitted criterion sheet are our additions. The source establishes that students find this use valuable; it establishes nothing about whether doing it in this order preserves the judgment better.

acts.na: Swap drafts and criterion sheets with a peer and review each other's against the same criteria. The disagreement-as-question rule and the retained sheet are unchanged.
rel: Exploring the affordances of generative AI in academic writing for students with disabilities: A bottom-up approach to inform GenAI policies
acts.sum: Before asking anything whether your draft meets the criteria, read the assessment criteria yourself and write one sentence per criterion saying where in your draft it is met and how. Where you cannot point to a location, mark it as unmet rather than arguing for it. This is the judgment the assignment is testing, and making it yourself first is what turns a later check into verification rather than substitution. If you then ask a tool to review your draft against the same criteria, compare its judgment with yours criterion by criterion, and treat every disagreement as a question rather than a correction. Where it says you have met something you marked unmet, go and look. Where it says you have missed something, decide whether it is right before changing anything. Submit your own criterion-by-criterion sheet alongside the work if your instructor allows it; it is evidence of the judgment you exercised.
acts.t: Read the Rubric Yourself Before Asking Whether You Answered It

The source argues directly against one-size-fits-all policy on those grounds, noting that applying identical standards and penalties to all students can be unfair. It also reports that 96 percent of respondents wanted involvement in shaping university AI policy, with many offering practical suggestions unprompted. The unfollowable-sentence method, the write-the-rule-you-could-follow step and the no-explanation rule are our additions. The 96 percent figure comes from a single survey item at one institution and the authors say so.

acts.sum: Read your course or institutional policy on AI use and mark every sentence you could not confidently follow. Not the ones you disagree with — the ones where you genuinely cannot tell whether a thing you do is permitted. Then write, in your own words, the rule you could follow: what you would disclose, when, and in what form, such that you would not be anxious about whether you had complied. Say what the existing wording does not cover that you actually do. Bring both to your instructor or to whoever collects student input on policy. If a rule turns out to be unfollowable for a reason that applies to more people than you, that is a finding about the rule rather than about you. Nothing in this activity requires you to say why a particular provision is hard for you, and you should not be asked.

acts.chg: The source's recommendation is specific and is followed closely. It names three levels of involvement — consultation, co-creation, and representation through central committee roles — and states two preconditions: that students with disabilities be fully respected and recognised as equal contributors rather than treated as passive subjects, and that they be provided with the institutional support, confidence and knowledge to participate effectively. The authors report that institutions often claim involvement while treating students as passive subjects, which is why this activity requires naming the level. They also report scepticism within higher education about whether these students can engage meaningfully with generative tools, and conclude from their own data and three other studies that the scepticism is unfounded. Working through the disability service is the source's own method for reaching participants. The change-record is ours.

acts.gate: The committee decides which of the three levels of student participation it is actually offering, says which, and records what changed as a result.
acts.na: The same three-level structure and two preconditions apply to any policy that constrains students. Nothing here is AI-specific except the subject of the policy.
rel: Exploring the affordances of generative AI in academic writing for students with disabilities: A bottom-up approach to inform GenAI policies
acts.sum: When your AI policy is written or revised, put the students it constrains on the panel rather than surveying them afterward. Decide first which of three levels you are actually offering, and say which: consultation, where students give feedback on a draft you control; co-creation, where they help write it; or representation, where a student sits on the body that decides. All three are legitimate and they are not the same, and claiming one while delivering another is worse than claiming none. Two conditions have to hold before it means anything. Students must be positioned as contributors whose judgment counts rather than as a group to be consulted about, and they must be given enough understanding of the tools to contribute informedly, which usually means offering training before the panel rather than expecting it. Work with your disability service to reach students who would not otherwise be asked. Record which level you offered and what changed as a result.
acts.t: Run the Policy Panel With the Affected Students On It

acts.chg: The source proposes three guiding principles for inclusive policy, and this activity implements two. The first is that policy must cover the entire lifecycle from training datasets through implementation to long-term monitoring, on the reasoning that bias and exclusion emerge early rather than in the output; that is the lifecycle instruction here. The third is that policies must be flexible and regularly audited, and the source names structured student panels, sandbox pilots with accessibility criteria to identify barriers before large-scale deployment, and participatory policy audits as the mechanisms. The named failure conditions, the deliberate recruitment, and the re-audit on update are our additions. The paid-tier criterion draws on the source's report that 19 percent of students with disabilities in a related UK study had paid for premium versions, which makes cost an access question rather than a convenience one.

acts.gate: The program decides what would count as the tool failing on access and what it would need to see before requiring it of students.
acts.na: The same sandbox, criteria and recruitment approach apply to any required platform or resource. The lifecycle framing is the part worth keeping regardless of technology.
rel: Exploring the affordances of generative AI in academic writing for students with disabilities: A bottom-up approach to inform GenAI policies
acts.sum: Before a generative tool becomes required or assumed in a course, pilot it in a bounded setting against access criteria you write down in advance. Decide beforehand what would count as failing: an interface that cannot be navigated without a mouse, output that cannot be read by a screen reader, a paid tier that gates the function that actually helps, a default that assumes a reading speed or an attention span. Recruit pilot participants deliberately rather than taking whoever volunteers, because the students most affected are the least likely to self-select. Look at the whole lifecycle rather than the output alone: what the tool was trained on, how it behaves in daily use, and what it does to people over a term. Record what you found and what you would need to see before requiring it. Audit again when the tool updates, because an accessible version does not stay accessible.

Day 1 goes to creating a ChatGPT account and playing with it for 15 minutes, discussing the responses that turn out interesting, and to writing a query script that gives ChatGPT a subject position and specific instructions to produce multiple counterclaims to your thesis. Unmündigkeit is unpacked as immaturity and, literally, 'mouthlessness', the inability to speak for oneself, and that term is what the remaining discussion turns on: what appropriate AI use looks like, and how to use AI without abdicating responsibility for public discourse. acts.sum: In the first week of a course, small groups each draft their own lists of acceptable and unacceptable AI uses for the assignments coming up, and those lists are put side by side so the class can build a single course AI policy out of them. The policy is not written once and filed: it comes back into view as each new assignment is introduced, or an AI Use Scale level is set per assignment instead. Drafting works from the institutional policy and the assignment descriptions, and stays inside what the institution requires and what consistency across sections demands. Instructors who have run it report that students sometimes settle on stricter rules than they would have set, alongside more dialogue about AI and less AI-based plagiarism — expectations end up clear because they are shared rather than announced.

Three questions organize the writing: 'Can we use GenAI, and how and when?', 'What counts as misuse?' and 'What are the consequences of misuse?' In the first you add probability weightings to a network of word-type nodes until the chain generates grammatical phrases; in the second you build a chain out of an existing text extract, drawing a [Start] box linked to the first word and then, for each 'current word', counting its occurrences and drawing weighted arrows to the words that follow, closing with a [Stop] box after the last word. You then interview the avatar as you would a focus group, flagging biased or stereotypical language where it appears, and adapt your argument to the audience the avatar describes — a profile, an annotated interview and an adapted plan that feed the multimodal argument coming next. Engineering the prompt is the skill in play, and the annotation is the check on it, since an avatar is a construction and noticing where the construction leans on stereotype is part of reading it.
acts.t: AI Audience Avatars for Multimodal Argument

acts.sum: Readings on LLMs, remix culture and plagiarism, among them Hutson 2021 in Nature, Ferguson's 'Everything Is a Remix', Knight 2019 and Teagarden 2019, set the ground before you bring an essay from a previous assignment to GPT-3.5 or GPT-4 at the end of the course. You put the common peer-review questions to it: whether the introduction supplies context, whether the thesis could be more specific, whether analysis follows the evidence, how the ideas progress, what would make the conclusion stronger. You also ask for linguistic analysis, describing a paragraph's tone or comparing tones across paragraphs. Its responses are weighed against human feedback and the most useful revision strategies applied. Closing out, you evaluate how the LLM supported your process and articulate an ethical framework for using it, so prompting skill and rhetorical judgment develop together.

srp: Identify benzene substitution patterns from measured infrared spectra while learning coding and model evaluation.

Students work through introductory Python and data-processing notebooks, interpolate and normalize spectra and inspect the 630–880 cm−1 region with PCA. They evaluate classification using 20 principal components over repeated 67:33 training/test splits, then collect two unknown spectra and classify them with the full-spectrum library.
Predicted ortho/meta/para assignments, visualized spectral structure and model-performance results.
Repeated holdout evaluation and comparison of known-label classifications; instructors and demonstrators support interpretation.
acts.sum: In this optional third-year chemistry practical, small groups of students learn data processing and machine-learning evaluation by identifying ortho, meta and para substitution patterns of benzene derivatives from infrared spectra. Working through introductory Python and Jupyter notebooks, students interpolate and normalize a labeled library of spectra, inspect the diagnostic region with principal component analysis, and evaluate a k-nearest-neighbors classifier over repeated training and test splits. They then measure two unknown samples on an ATR infrared spectrometer and classify them against the full-spectrum library. The classifier supplies predicted labels; students judge its performance from held-out results, with demonstrators supporting interpretation. The outcome is a set of predicted assignments, visualized spectral structure and model-performance results.
acts.t: Classify measured infrared spectra to identify regioisomers in a Python machine-learning practical
acts.tool: Python; Jupyter notebooks; pandas; PCA; k-nearest neighbors; ATR infrared spectrometer

acts.sum: Physics educators describe how to build an affordable self-driving optical laboratory in which a machine-learning controller tries to reproduce a target light spectrum through repeated measurement. An LED array driven by an Arduino and a digital-to-analog converter shines into a light-tight enclosure where a spectral sensor records the result; after calibration, voltage–spectrum data are collected and used to train models. srp: Estimate a target causal parameter while using ML to fit nuisance functions.

Researchers define outcome, treatment, covariates and the target parameter in a DoubleML data object, choose a supported model and nuisance learners, fit using sample splitting and cross-fitting, and inspect the estimate, standard error and confidence interval, using the worked example as a reproducibility check.
An estimated effect with inferential uncertainty.
Runnable examples and simulation-based demonstrations; identification remains the researcher's responsibility.
acts.sum: An economist or statistician estimating a causal effect uses the DoubleML Python package so that flexible machine-learning models can be used without biasing the estimate of the target parameter. Following a tutorial built on a published lung atlas, the researcher registers raw counts and batch covariates, fits the scVI variational model, and inspects latent neighbors, clusters and visualizations; scANVI can optionally be initialized from the same model with supplied cell-type labels. acts.sum: An analyst who needs to find records referring to the same person or entity across files without a shared unique identifier uses Splink, an open-source probabilistic record-linkage library. The analyst defines blocking rules that limit which pairs are compared and specifies how fields such as names and dates are compared; the software estimates prior and non-match parameters and uses expectation maximization to learn match parameters without labeled training data, then predicts a match probability for each candidate pair. acts.sum: Before retraining a classifier, an analyst uses cleanlab to find training examples whose labels are probably wrong. The analyst generates out-of-sample predicted class probabilities through cross-validation, runs cleanlab's data and label issue detection to rank suspect examples by estimated label quality, and then inspects and corrects the flagged labels or compares a workflow that prunes them. The corrected or pruned data are used to retrain the model, and performance is compared on separately evaluated data. A model's disagreement with a label is a reason to look rather than proof of an annotation error, so the analyst's review of flagged examples against independent evidence is the step that decides. The tutorial uses a small synthetic four-class dataset and can simulate perfect human correction, which a real review does not guarantee.
acts.t: Audit noisy labels using out-of-sample predictions and human review

acts.sum: Researchers in social work and human-computer interaction use anchored topic modeling to examine how risk, protective, systemic and procedural factors interact across the case histories of families in a family-preservation program. Case notes are arranged chronologically, cleaned and anonymized; researchers read sample histories and use a socioecological framework to choose anchor words that steer Anchored CorEx toward domain-relevant topics. They fit and compare models, then several authors interpret topics independently before reconciling labels and using axial coding to relate them, and they compare topic patterns across normalized segments of each history. acts.risk: The source reports reproduction of Western cultural stereotypes and symbolic oversimplification in the images.
srp: To evaluate the theological, symbolic and pedagogical value of AI-generated biblical imagery and determine the didactic potential and limits of DALL-E images in Bible teaching.

The authors generated images of two biblical scenes with DALL-E 3 in ChatGPT-4o using a vague prompt and then a targeted prompt naming Catholic symbolism and educational use, kept the first output of each, and compared the pairs for theological depth, symbolic coherence and stereotyping and against sacred art.
Paired images per scene and a written evaluation of their theological, symbolic and didactic adequacy.
Comparison with selected works of sacred art.
acts.sum: Before using AI images in Bible teaching, you select scenes deeply rooted in Christian iconography; the source used the Baptism of Jesus and the Last Supper. For each, you issue a deliberately vague prompt first, to see which iconographic patterns the image system produces by default, and then a targeted prompt that adds explicit references to Catholic symbolism and states the religious-education purpose. You keep the first image returned for each prompt, with no refinement, and compare the pair for narrative or interpretive character, theological depth, symbolic coherence and Western cultural stereotyping, and against selected works of sacred art. The teacher must judge whether either image is theologically adequate for teaching and turn the comparison into didactic recommendations. In the source, both tiers showed shallow theology, symbolic oversimplification and Western stereotypes.
acts.t: Two-tiered prompt audit of AI-generated biblical scene images before using them in teaching

acts.rf: Critical reflection on generative AI in biblical interpretation.
srp: To develop students' religious visual literacy and critical thinking about generative AI in biblical interpretation by detecting and repairing faults in an AI-generated image.

Religion teachers treat AI-generated biblical images as starting points and guide students in identifying inconsistencies (symbolic dispersion), correcting them, and situating elements accurately within the biblical context.
A student critical analysis naming, correcting and contextualizing inconsistencies in an AI-generated image.
Students situate each element within the narrative, historical and cultural context of the passage.
acts.sum: A religion teacher presents an AI-generated image of a biblical scene as material to be examined rather than as an illustration, and introduces the idea of symbolic dispersion: religious elements added without regard to narrative, historical or cultural context. The source's examples are a cross in the background of the Last Supper and the inscription "Ecce Agnus Dei" in a baptism scene. Students identify the inconsistencies in the image, say how each should be corrected, and place each element accurately within the biblical passage. The student must judge each element against the biblical text and its historical setting. The exercise ends in reflection on how generative AI handles biblical interpretation. The source calls this visual debugging and frames it as turning students from observers into interpreters.
acts.t: Visual debugging: students correct symbolic dispersion in AI biblical images

acts.sum: Students first describe what is happening in an AI-generated image of a biblical scene, consider what each figure might be communicating, and propose additions or changes. They compare the image with classical artworks, the source names Verrocchio and da Vinci, to see the theological depth and symbolic richness the AI image lacks. Students then generate their own AI illustrations of biblical passages, compare and critique them, and improve them over several rounds of deliberate, reflective prompting. The student must distinguish what is merely pleasing to look at from what is theologically meaningful, which the source calls the sensus theologicus. The model supplies rapid, adaptable illustrations; the sacred art and the biblical text supply the standard.

srp: To assess whether chatbot-assisted learning, used alongside conventional teaching, improves dental students' comprehension of intraoral radiographic techniques.

After a standardized lecture and baseline test, the chatbot group receives an orientation and a standardized prompt set, studies with a fixed model version through individual accounts for four weeks with unlimited follow-up questions but no sharing of outputs, submits compiled transcripts for specialist review, and sits a blueprint-matched post-test.

acts.sum: After a standard two-hour lecture on intraoral radiographic techniques, dental students study the material with ChatGPT over four weeks. A specialist gives them an orientation on using the chatbot and a standardized set of prompts covering every component of the techniques, and everyone uses the same model version through individual accounts. Students may ask any follow-up questions to clarify doubts but are asked not to share generated responses with each other. At the end they compile and submit their chat transcripts through the institutional learning platform, where the specialist checks them for adherence to the prompt set. Knowledge is measured with blueprint-matched multiple-choice tests after the lecture and after four weeks. The specialist, not the chatbot, is the reference for what counts as correct technique.

acts.sum: A veterinary communication team builds standardized clients for communication labs with free ChatGPT. For each case you fill a fixed prompt template with the owner's name, ethnicity, location and rural or urban setting, language, occupation, household, the animal's type, name and age, the reason for the visit, and socioeconomic or cultural factors. srp: To use ChatGPT as a virtual peer in flipped anatomy instruction, supporting content review, group learning and reflective thinking while building critical evaluation and digital literacy.

After pre-class H5P videos, groups of about six use ChatGPT in class only, prompting in Spanish or English, through three phases: evaluate accuracy of responses (vomeronasal organ), critique flawed explanations (ductus and truncus arteriosus), and apply comparative anatomy to a problem (aortic arch). acts.sum: In a first-year veterinary anatomy course taught as a flipped classroom, students prepare with interactive videos and then work in class in groups of about six, with ChatGPT as a virtual group member used only during those sessions. Students write their own questions for it in Spanish or English. In the first phase, on the vomeronasal organ, they pick out the relevant anatomical data and judge whether the chatbot's answers are accurate. In the second, on congenital heart anomalies, they critique flawed AI explanations and sharpen their own understanding. In the third, on the aortic arch, they apply comparative anatomy to a complex problem. Students must hold their own anatomical knowledge as the standard against which the chatbot's answers are judged. Understanding is assessed through leveled questions, including one on chatbot use, embedded in the formal exams.
acts.t: ChatGPT as a virtual group member across three Bloom-aligned phases in flipped veterinary anatomy

acts.sum: Working in groups, you choose three socially or politically charged identity labels, such as "refugee" or "scientist," and note the prejudices attached to each. You generate three to five photographic portraits per label with a text-to-image platform of your choice, vary the prompts by age, gender or race, and document how small changes alter the images. You then gather existing portraits of the same categories from art history, social media, popular culture and news media, and identify visual patterns, typologies and prejudices across both sets. You present a critical reflection to the class and submit a written one relating what you found to course readings on the face, facial recognition and AI-generated images, and you must be able to justify your platform choice. A class discussion then weighs each group's findings and the limits of bias correction.

In the first phase the instructor explains political communication online and the manipulation of the electoral public sphere, then gives a pretest in which students judge ten Twitter accounts as automated or not. acts.sum: When you review a manuscript or grant proposal, you first check the reviewer AI policy of the journal, publisher or funder and follow the most restrictive rule that applies; if AI is prohibited, you do not use it. Where it is permitted, you use only a system that preserves confidentiality, such as one hosted locally or by a trustworthy institution, and never upload the manuscript, any part of it, or your review comments to a cloud tool, even for language editing. The permitted system may summarize the manuscript and improve the wording of your review, on the assumption that it will make mistakes. You watch for hidden prompts planted by authors, check every AI-generated passage for accuracy, currency and bias, disclose the use and its purposes, and keep full responsibility for the review's judgments.

acts.sum: Academic developers running an accredited certificate in teaching, learning and assessment build hands-on generative AI trials into three modules. In one, participants read an article unaided before class, then in class upload it to a document chatbot, obtain a summary, and compare it with their own understanding. In another, pairs upload an article on learning theories and ask the bot to describe the four theories, then skim the article to judge the summary's accuracy; the bot returned three rather than four, which became the discussion point about limitations. acts.sum: A program director reviews every module in a degree program against a framework of four AI literacy dimensions: know and understand AI, use and apply AI, evaluate and create with AI, and AI ethics. acts.sum: The Co-Creative Mentoring Model pairs educators as mentors and mentees and works through four phases. In Preparation, facilitators scaffold readiness for gender-responsive, AI-enhanced teaching. In Co-Creation, each pair uses ChatGPT to generate lesson prompts, assessments and simplified content and Canva to create accessible visuals, receives feedback, and produces open educational resources that are evaluated for inclusivity and freedom from bias. In Implementation the resources are used in teaching, and in the Sustainability and Reflection phase peer mentoring is established and OER sharing promoted. The model was run with 23 participants from Ghanaian colleges of education, basic schools and regulatory agencies; participants named the hands-on co-creation sessions as the most valuable part, and limited training time and internet connectivity as the main obstacles.
acts.t: Four-phase mentor-mentee pairing that co-creates inclusive open resources with ChatGPT and Canva

acts.sum: For open and distance learning, this design builds an authentic assessment that states in writing exactly which uses of generative AI learners may make. The instructor makes the task as context-specific as possible, provides a rubric of requirements and criteria for each section, and hands learners one of several scope statements, for example that AI may be used for planning, idea development and research as long as the final submission shows how ideas were developed and refined, or that it may assist with drafting and refining provided learners critically evaluate and modify what it produces. The task is broken into parts sequenced across a semester, learners self-assess and cite the page numbers where evidence of each requirement appears, and reflection, disclosure and demonstration of process serve as accountability. The booklet cautions that using GenAI to mark student work currently carries more risk than benefit.
acts.t: Authentic assessment designed with an explicit, written scope for permitted student GenAI use

acts.sum: In a distance-learning Java programming course, the course coordinator builds a practice application in which GPT-4, reached through an API, returns immediate feedback on students' code. Rather than accepting open-ended work, the application offers predefined tasks mapped to the same skill taxonomy and criteria as the graded assignment, and evaluates each submission for correctness, coding style, efficiency and adherence to good practice, pitching explanations to the learner's level: foundational explanations and error analysis for beginners, optimization suggestions for more advanced learners. acts.sum: Starting from the claim that poor generative AI results often stem from poor prompts, the authors propose treating quality prompts as open educational resources. Faculty and other experts write prompts for their domain, release them under an open license, and deposit them in a shared online prompt bank built to be sustainable. Experts from various fields enrich the bank, quality assurance procedures check the validity and robustness of prompts, and users rate the prompts they reuse so future users can see quality and administrators can spot low-quality entries and request revisions. Teachers and students both reuse prompts from the bank in their own contexts. The authors add that open frameworks for writing prompts, especially for domain-specific knowledge, could improve results. The article presents this as a proposed scenario rather than a reported implementation.
acts.t: Openly licensed, rated prompt bank maintained as a shared educational resource

acts.sum: Before putting generative AI output into an openly licensed resource, a faculty author runs a due-diligence check for infringement of individual protected works. The first step is to read the prompt critically: a prompt aimed at a trademarked character invites infringement, while prompts for an abstract book cover with a beach and a whale or a three-paragraph description of hydrocarbons are unlikely to. For text output, the author searches the web to make sure the exact language does not already exist in copyrighted content; for images, they run a reverse image search with a tool such as TinEye or Google Images. Output with no identical match is treated as likely includable; output that matches a protected work is not used. The guidance notes that US copyright does not protect styles or ideas and points to fair-use codes for OER.
acts.t: Infringement due-diligence check on generative AI output before it goes into an open resource

acts.sum: UNESCO's AI competency framework for students gives a matrix of assessment task types crossed with three progression levels (Understand, Apply, Create). For the human-centered mindset aspect the task types are conflict-based opinion taking, critical evaluation and social interactions; for the ethics of AI they are scenario-based value orientation, ethical behaviors and rule-making. An instructor picks an aspect and a level, pairs a paper or computer-based test on the main points of that competency block with open questions that put a contested claim to students, and adapts those questions to the local context. Sample items ask whether artificial general intelligence will arrive by 2030, whether students still need to learn to draft reports if AI drafts meeting minutes, and whether AI will enhance or threaten inclusion locally. Students answer by stating, evaluating and analyzing positions; no AI tool is used.
acts.t: Conflict-based and scenario-based assessment tasks built from a competency-by-level matrix

acts.sum: A medical educator developing an Objective Structured Clinical Examination station uses an existing, validated standardized-patient checklist as a template. The educator uploads the published checklist, from a neonatal jaundice case in the source, into ChatGPT and prompts it to produce an analogous checklist for a different clinical presentation, a child with asthma. The model infers the structure, granularity and item style of the template and returns a draft, thirty items in the source. The educator then reviews the draft for clinical accuracy and for fit with the trainees' level before any use; the source attaches a caveat that clinician review for medical accuracy is required to every OSCE task it lists. The output is a draft checklist for a new station that becomes usable only after that review.

acts.sum: Before any student meets a nursing chatbot simulation, faculty evaluate the prompt that configures it. The first phase of the AIMS framework scores the prompt on six instructional domains using a 0-2 rubric: clinical and content credibility; alignment with the educational objectives and intended cognitive level; persona clarity, meaning whether the bot's role and tone are defined; inclusivity and cultural competence of the scenario and language; transparency about the AI's identity to learners; and personalization to learner needs. Domains that score low point to revisions in the prompt before deployment and before Phase 2, which evaluates the chatbot in live interaction. The authors state that prompt design is where inaccurate, biased or unsafe interactions can be prevented, and they also demonstrated automating the scoring with a GPT-4.0-based Eval-Bot v1.
acts.t: Pre-deployment review of an AI simulation prompt against six instructional domains (AIMS Phase 1)

acts.sum: Once a nursing chatbot simulation has passed prompt review, its behavior in live interaction is scored. Faculty rate eight criteria on the same 0-2 rubric used in the framework's first phase: credibility and accuracy, user experience, feedback and assessment quality, user agency, equity and accessibility, transparency, learning outcomes, and interactivity quality. The authors also ran an automated evaluator, Eval-Bot v1 built on OpenAI GPT-4.0, over the same criteria, and had three experienced nursing faculty review independently so the two sets of scores could be compared to surface disagreement and reduce bias. The output is a scored performance evaluation of the deployed simulation with automated and human scores side by side, used to decide whether the simulation performs acceptably in use and not only on paper.

acts.sum: Each student picks a professional role in a hospital crisis (ER Charge Nurse, Facilities Coordinator, Informatics Lead, Communications Officer or Physician) and responds to an escalating scenario in which the power fails, patients keep arriving and equipment breaks down. The student types decisions in role, such as sending an emergency message to staff or assessing ventilator patients. The chatbot, configured by faculty with a documented prompt structure covering roles, escalation phases and debriefing rules, acts as scenario engine: it presents time-sensitive prompts and raises complexity across defined phases. The authors wrote system prompts for three culturally grounded scenarios in ChatGPT (GPT-4.1) and refined them through a five-student pilot; 24 second-cycle nursing students completed a pre-simulation self-assessment, a 10-15 minute individual conversation with the AI patient, a post-simulation assessment and eight open-ended reflection questions, followed by debriefing.

acts.sum: Faculty write a system prompt for each of three clinical scenarios that fixes the AI patient's cultural background, communication norms, behavioral tendencies, emotional tone and clinical context; one is Kenji, a 72-year-old Japanese man after colectomy who avoids eye contact and minimizes his pain in keeping with meiwaku, the avoidance of burdening others. A small pilot is used to refine realism and emotional appropriateness. Each nursing student completes a cultural-competence self-assessment, then holds an individual 10 to 15 minute conversation with the AI patient, working to build rapport, identify culturally shaped needs, recognize communication barriers and propose culturally appropriate interventions. A post-simulation assessment, eight open-ended reflection questions and a debrief follow. The authors describe the realism as cognitive-emotional and linguistic rather than embodied.
acts.t: Culturally grounded AI patient encounters for nursing cultural competence

acts.sum: An instructor and a teaching assistant build a classroom card game on international trade and population health for fifteen sovereign states. They use ChatGPT to compile historical health-affecting events, build economic profiles with GDP, per-capita indicators and import-export portfolios, decide which resources each state starts with and must obtain, and run repeated simulations to check that the allocations could realistically be met through trade. Adobe Firefly generates deliberately generic imagery for resource and event cards, avoiding identifiable people or places. Every country-specific figure is then cross-checked against authoritative sources, every card is reviewed for biased or stereotyped portrayals, images are screened for appropriateness, and the whole game is playtested by people a month before the pilot. The output is a complete, playable set of state profiles, resource and event cards, and trading rules.

acts.sum: In a 75-minute undergraduate public health class, groups of two or three represent sovereign states, dividing the roles of Trade Representative, Health Minister and Finance Minister. Each group holds three to ten resource cards according to its nation's GDP and must meet its health needs through trade. Three ten-minute rounds stand for 2018, 2019 and 2020; trading starts among designated partners and opens more widely at the end of each round, and the 2020 round simulates the COVID-19 pandemic with heavy restrictions. The instructor plays the US Trade Representative and the teaching assistant plays US aid agencies, introducing event cards and observing against the learning objectives. Reflection runs between rounds, by regional bloc and as a class debrief, followed by a written reflection within 48 hours. Students are told the background data and graphics were AI-assisted.

After lectures on digital communication, an AI and LLM primer, chatbots and AR/VR, students are given a health-department HIV-prevention scenario and build a simple PrEP-inquiry chatbot in Botpress's graphical interface, constructing its conversation workflow, and present their materials in week ten.

acts.sum: In a graduate digital health communication course, public health students build a simple chatbot that would let health-department clients ask about pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) by text message. Working in Botpress, a chatbot development platform whose basic tools are free, students construct the conversation flow in the platform's graphical interface, deciding how the bot greets a client, which questions it can handle and how each exchange proceeds. The lab sits alongside new lectures on one-way versus two-way digital communication, a primer on AI and large language model concepts pitched at students with limited statistical background, chatbots, and augmented and virtual reality. Students present their health communication materials in the final week of the ten-week course. The chatbot is the artifact students design, so the judgment about what it should say is theirs.
acts.t: Graduate lab in which public health students build a PrEP inquiry chatbot in Botpress for a health department scenario

Two human assessors screened titles and abstracts without AI; data extraction ran three parallel ChatGPT rounds per article in separate conversations with GPT-4 and GPT-4o; a third human reviewer consolidated human and AI responses, verified that no information was omitted or spuriously generated, and determined final answers; ROBINS-I quality assessment was human; accuracy was compared with chi-square tests.

acts.sum: In a systematic review of virtual patients for clinical reasoning, the review team divides work between people and ChatGPT and then measures the result. Title and abstract screening is done by two independent human reviewers with no AI involvement. For data extraction, each included article goes through three parallel ChatGPT extraction rounds, each in a separate conversation to expose response variability, using both GPT-4 and GPT-4o, for defined categories: software or AI used, participant numbers, clinical area, learning impact and student satisfaction. A third human reviewer consolidates the human and model extractions, checks that nothing was omitted or spuriously generated, and sets every final answer before accuracy is rated. Quality appraisal with ROBINS-I stays human work, and the extraction accuracy of each model and each human reviewer is compared with chi-square tests.

You prepare the corpus, choose a cloud or local GPU, and fine-tune the model with the aitextgen library. You then prompt it with questions such as "What is Brexit?" and sentence stems such as "Theresa May is" and "Boris Johnson is", generating five samples per prompt. acts.sum: This Programming Historian lesson builds a Naive Bayes classifier over the Old Bailey Online archive of London criminal trials from 1674 to 1913. Because every trial is annotated in XML with offense, verdict and witness details, the archive supplies a human standard: you download the trials, create cross-validation samples, train and test the classifier, and check its category assignments against the curators' annotation, then extract the features most indicative of each category. The lesson then turns to the errors. The scripts save false positives and "close relatives", trials the classifier narrowly excluded from a category, into separate files, and you read those borderline trials to ask why the classifier grouped them as it did and what that says about how offense categories shaded into one another. The historian judges what counts as a useful classification.
acts.t: Train a classifier on annotated criminal trial records, validate it against human annotation, then read the misclassifications as history

acts.sum: Working from digitized college yearbooks, one per decade from 1911 to 1961, you set up a Python environment in Google Colab, convert the PDFs to images, detect faces with OpenCV Haar cascades, extract each face, and run the pre-trained DeepFace model to classify smiles. You then compare smile frequency across the decades against a published argument that early sitters avoided smiling to look dignified while later amateur photography brought more smiles. You interpret the counts with that failure pattern and the dataset's composition in view.

acts.sum: Because logistics often limit interview practice, students rehearse ethnographic interviewing with a generative AI prompt that simulates an informant. They adjust the prompt so the informant represents different cultural backgrounds or social positions, such as a rural elder or a migrant household, and repeat interviews across scenarios. Small groups then analyze the transcripts, looking for cultural subtleties in the model's answers and for places where it fails to convey genuine human diversity, which the course links to algorithmic bias. acts.sum: In a translation course, students translate an assigned Arabic source text into German on their own, using dictionaries and reference books, before they see any machine output. They then set their version beside a translation of the same text produced by ChatGPT and assess the differences in vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, idioms and collocations. The instructor leads a class discussion in which students explain why the model may have chosen particular words, phrases or sentences and weigh those contextual choices against their own translation decisions. The student must be able to defend or revise each of their own choices with reasons, rather than defer to the machine version. The cycle recurs every two weeks across a fifteen-week semester, with the same texts given to a comparison group that works without AI and receives instructor feedback instead.

acts.sum: In an integrated content-and-language course, law students first study the structure of an international legal document, including the legal systems of the participating countries, and the vocabulary and grammar used in drafting such documents. The instructor explains the goals, stages and deadlines of the AI-based practice and leads a discussion of information security, authorial ethics and why unauthorized borrowing from generative AI is not acceptable. acts.sum: In a sound recording seminar, the class first learns about field recording, the soundwalk format, and the privacy and ethical risks of using a proprietary AI agent. The group then names sounds they consider typical of their campus and its surroundings. The instructor turns the list into a prompt, runs it in ChatGPT on a projected screen, and the class critiques each version of the resulting narration and decides the next instruction. In the source, students asked for an emotional arc, found the result too emotive and short on specific sounds, and went back to the first version with an instruction to shorten it. Each student then has four days to realize the agreed script as a three-to-five-minute stereo soundwalk, recording most sounds themselves and using as much or as little of the text as they choose, for playback and discussion.

acts.sum: The instructor first gives a conventional lecture on the myth of Medea from a mythology dictionary entry with translated ancient sources, pointing out that the infanticide central to Euripides is absent from earlier versions, where Hesiod and Pindar present Medea as Jason's helper. He then asks ChatGPT for a summary of the myth and has students analyze it. Students find that it standardizes the myth around its most canonical versions, Euripides and Apollonius of Rhodes, and omits the alternatives that circulated in antiquity. The instructor then asks for a detailed academic account, in which the archaic versions are still missing, and finally asks directly for the different ancient versions, which the model then lists chronologically. Students see that the omissions depend on how the question was asked.

srp: To teach creative writing through alternate history by having students direct a generative model across ideation, structure and style, while challenging the tendency to accept its first response.

The instructor demonstrates live prompting with collective analysis. Students build a persona for the model, request five scenarios, have it outline a seven-part plan, critique the plan themselves and then ask the model for feedback, produce pastiches, apply quantified stylistic constraints, and compose transitions manually or in a separate dialogue with context restated; they submit the structuring task and the final story.

acts.sum: In a second-year applied literary studies course, students write alternate-history ('uchronian') short stories of up to 7,000 words, some reimagining ancient myths, such as Ariadne taking revenge on Theseus. The instructor projects ChatGPT and enters prompts live, analyzing each output with the class to challenge the habit of accepting the first response. Students give the model a persona as author-narrator with a defined role, task and audience, ask for five different step-by-step scenarios and choose one, and have it outline a seven-part plan. They critique that plan themselves before asking the model for its own numbered critique. In drafting, they prompt for pastiche of a named author and impose quantified style constraints, such as proportions of description, dialogue and narration, and they write the transitions between generated sections themselves. The plan and the final story are each graded against a grid.
acts.t: Writing an alternate-history retelling of an ancient myth by directing a persona-configured chatbot

They write down what they expect, run the code on a small test dataset and compare. srp: As the source frames it, to give librarians a standardized method for constructing prompts that produce consistent, precise outputs by reusing a framework they already use daily.

The librarian fills the Task, Context, Example, Persona, Format and Tone slots for an information request, assembles them into a prose prompt as a research question is formed from a PICO instance, and for a related request swaps out only the changed component.
A completed six-slot table, the assembled prompt, and an AI output tailored to the requester.
acts.sum: A health sciences librarian turns an incoming information request into a prompt the way a PICO question is built from a clinical scenario. You fill six slots: Task (what is to be identified), Context (population, condition or scope), Example (the kind of instance to focus on), Persona (who the output is for and why), Format (for instance a detailed paragraph with subheadings) and Tone (for instance professional and thorough). You assemble the slots into one prose prompt in a logical order and submit it. For a related later request you change only the slot that differs and keep the rest. The source works through two scenarios, a physician asking about complications of type 2 diabetes in older patients and a faculty member preparing a lecture on sleep disorders and adolescent mental health. The librarian remains answerable for what is passed on to the requester.
acts.t: Building a librarian's reference prompt from a PICO-style slot framework (Task, Context, Example, Persona, Format, Tone)

srp: To enable students to determine the extent to which a claim in their text is supported by the content of the cited source.

Students apply four stages to each citation that brings forward specific content: consolidation (citation, bibliography, existence and retrievability of the record), textual entailment, validity in the cited context, and transferability to the citing context; a draft set of stacking exercises walks through the steps.

acts.sum: Students learn a four-stage procedure for checking whether a claim in a text is actually warranted by the source it cites. In consolidation they confirm that each in-text citation matches a bibliography entry, that every entry is cited, that the item matches a record that does or did exist, and that the record is retrievable. In textual entailment they look in the cited work for content that supports or contradicts the claim. In validity they judge whether that content is empirically warranted in its own study, and in transferability whether it carries over to the citing context. The instructor supplies reading on why authors cite and a set of stacking exercises that, the authors state, show the fragility of argument in the record and the instability of chatbot results.
acts.t: Four-stage citation validation protocol for checking whether a citing claim is warranted by its source

acts.sum: Across a fifteen-week module in a prototype undergraduate syllabus, students translate a critical theoretical framework into executable instructions for a language model. They first write a framework selection memo and an annotated bibliography, then decompose the theory into operational primitives, each with action verbs, the textual evidence it maps to and edge cases, and reflect on which concepts were hardest to operationalize. Next they write system instructions with a persona, contextual grounding, the primitives as explicit instructions, negative constraints and a required output structure, test them on a sample text, and keep a prompt journal logging every version and its rationale, including failed prompts and why they failed. acts.sum: After establishing that AI content can look accurate and appropriate without being so, the instructor models a critical analysis and sets it as a learning activity. Students apply four considerations: content accuracy checked against trusted resources, bias awareness, ethical considerations and source verification. They then work through two question banks. About the tool: who created and trained it, on what dataset, under what privacy policy, with what limitations, and who is harmed or benefits. About the text: what is present and missing, word choices, audience, reliability, sources and biases. Students close by searching the internet for the original sources the tool may have drawn on. The output is a written analysis of the tool and its text.
acts.t: Critical Media Literacy Questions for Interrogating an AI Writing Tool and Its Text

acts.sum: After completing an assignment in which they used a generative AI tool, students reflect in writing or discussion on three clusters of questions. Under tool effectiveness they characterize how accurate, precise and contextualized the responses were and whether the tool hallucinated. Under critical evaluation they describe how they decided which responses to trust, when the tool seemed most reliable, and whether prior knowledge of the topic is needed to use it. Under usage they identify which prompts produced the best and worst responses, when the tool got caught in a loop, and what they would recommend to next year's students. Before assigning it, the instructor reviews the assignment's learning objectives to decide whether a metacognitive component serves them and how reflections will be shared. srp: To support students during a remote titration experiment and to characterize the learning needs that arise and the roles students assign to the assistant.

acts.sum: First-year students in an introductory chemistry course carry out an acid-base titration on a remote laboratory platform, following a two-part activity document that frames the task with a histology-related problem. During the second part, which uses acetic acid, they can consult by chat an assistant built on GPT-4o that instructors have supplied with laboratory descriptions, procedural guidance, safety information and excerpts from their lab manual. The assistant has no internet access and is instructed not to give complete numerical solutions, so students record burette volumes, compute molar concentration, pH and unit conversions, and write conclusions themselves. Consulting the assistant is optional. The output is the student's measurements, calculations and a laboratory report with tables and conclusions; the study grouped student queries into experiment operation, data processing, conceptual understanding and report guidance.

acts.sum: Before a remote chemistry laboratory runs, instructors configure the AI assistant students will be able to consult. Through the platform's configuration interface they enter information about the laboratory setup, instruments and safety guidelines, add excerpts from their own laboratory manual as the assistant's context, and write behavioral constraints, most notably that the assistant must not give complete numerical solutions. The assistant, built on GPT-4o, has no internet access and answers only text questions related to the experiment. Once deployed alongside the experiment, its interactions with students are logged by the platform for later analysis. The instructor's judgment lies in what context to supply and what the assistant must refuse to do, so that it supports reasoning without doing the calculations students are meant to perform.
acts.t: Instructor configuration of a laboratory-scoped AI assistant with behavioral constraints

acts.sum: An environmental data science course for upper-level undergraduate and graduate students balances AI-assisted work against assessment that shows what students can do without it, through four components. In the first nine lessons students learn Python basics through two assignments completed without AI assistance. Formal guidance on AI tools, prompting and responsible use follows mid-course, and from lesson ten students complete project-based assignments and a term project on datasets of their own interest with AI coding assistance, documenting their AI use. A 75-minute paper-based in-class exam tests conceptual understanding with AI prohibited. Multi-step case studies, such as the effect of COVID-19 on air quality, let AI help with processing while students connect the steps and interpret the results themselves. The outcome is a graded portfolio spanning all four components.

acts.sum: In an environmental data science course, students work multi-step case studies on real datasets, such as the effect of COVID-19 on air quality in South Florida or changes in rainfall under different CMIP6 future scenarios for North and South Florida. In class they first derive the least-squares formulation themselves, then spend 45 minutes conveying the problem to the chatbot step by step, breaking the equations into parts, to generate MATLAB code. Before each reply to the model, the team must deliberate and agree on its answer, so the reasoning is argued out among students. The model's questions challenge assumptions and ask for elaboration, and the team refines its explanation in response. srp: To assess how effectively chatbots solve statistical problems, understand the causes of their errors, and derive recommendations for integrating them in education.

Faculty collected the validated 54-question exam bank with expert answers, checked item integrity, presented 52 questions (156 items) to ChatGPT 3.5 three times each in randomized order, compared responses with expert answers and categorized errors, then interviewed chatbots on the 36 error-containing questions, confronting one chatbot with another's response.

acts.sum: Statistics faculty test how chatbots perform on the validated final-exam question bank of an undergraduate statistics course for engineering students. They first check the items for missing special characters, formulas or tables, confirm the chatbot understands the questions, and then present 52 questions, 156 items in all, to ChatGPT 3.5 three times each in randomized order. Every answer is compared with the expert professors' answers, and each error is categorized by statistical field and sub-field, question type, reason and reasoning complexity. In a second, qualitative stage the 36 questions with errors are taken into semi-structured interviews with chatbots using a grounded-theory approach, including confrontations in which one chatbot's answer is put to another and agreement, disagreement and revision are analyzed. The result is an error profile and categories of chatbot behavior under challenge.
acts.t: Auditing a statistics final exam against chatbots and cross-examining chatbots on their errors

acts.sum: Outside its project phase, an undergraduate engineering probability and statistics course has students work basic probability, combinatorics and Gaussian interval problems by hand or with a calculator, without notes, and learn thumb rules for one- and two-standard-deviation intervals. The stated purpose is confidence in the principles and a simple reference against which to check whether a computational tool is being used correctly. The authors tie this to generative AI: because AI can now write the code for such tools, checking tool usage against a hand-worked answer matters more. Their example is MATLAB's erf() function, whose two-sided definition requires scaling inputs by one over the square root of two before Z-score use. Later in the term the course shifts to team machine-learning projects in Python on real datasets.
acts.t: Hand-worked solutions as the check on tool and AI-written code in engineering statistics

acts.sum: In an introductory engineering course, students write a series of individual reports of increasing complexity on the results of hands-on class activities such as friction measurement and bridge design and testing. Each report follows a provided template, so structure is given rather than invented, and reports stay individual even when the project was done in teams. The grading rubric ignores grammar and spelling unless comprehension suffers. Students are encouraged to use generative AI to improve their writing on condition that they cite any AI tools used, and may openly submit an AI-enhanced version for an improved grade. Feedback on one report is meant to carry into the next. The authors argue the incentive to cheat is low because no single report weighs much and each rests on the class's own data.

acts.sum: In a 60-minute episode of a machine-learning workshop for biologists, learners choose a published paper that uses supervised learning, either from a supplied list of biology and ecology papers or one of their own, and read it in advance. Together they examine a partially completed example chart, find in the paper where each filled entry came from, and complete its conclusions section. In groups they then fill a blank chart for their chosen paper, describing how machine learning is used at each stage, and reach a conclusion about whether the claims made with machine learning are valid. The episode draws out that published machine-learning workflows are often non-linear and that papers often omit details needed to evaluate them.

acts.sum: Instructors in a doctoral-level molecular biology course test how a widely available model performs on their own take-home experimental-design assignments. Each question is assigned a Bloom's level with the Blooming Biology Tool. Student responses are sampled at random from a cohort that finished before ChatGPT's release, so none could have used it. GPT-4o answers every item, ten times for each multiple-choice question, and free responses are generated and then rewritten in paragraph form so their style matches student writing. Three graders score all responses blind against a standardized rubric, and performance is compared by Bloom's level to locate the items most exposed to the tool. Student answers are graded alongside the model's, not given to it. In the source, students outperformed the model overall, which was weakest at the remember and apply levels.

acts.sum: Having mapped where a model underperforms on their course assignments, life-science instructors design new questions that require inference from real experimental images. For a poorly annotated four-lane DNA footprinting gel, students identify the technique, describe its key steps and interpret each lane as a condition or control; other items pair an image with multiple-choice options so a vague answer is not possible. The instructors test the new items against GPT-4o, including a version without the image, to see how much the image carries the question. They also revise rubrics so graders have the ideal answer, only the first experiment a student proposes is graded, and the choice of technique must be justified, and they weight take-home work toward applying known procedures in new situations. The source reports much lower model scores on image-inference items than on control questions.
acts.t: Redesigning life science assessment around graph and gel interpretation the model cannot do

srp: Investigate the potential of generative AI in engineering laboratory instruction using a standard soil mechanics experiment.

Both groups received identical instruction; the AI group could consult freely available generative AI tools during experimental operation, raw-data processing and report writing, while the traditional group used textbooks; assessment combined team operation, individual report and team presentation with peer questioning.
Experimental operation performance, an individual laboratory report and a team presentation with defense, scored on six indicators.
acts.sum: In a third-year hydraulic engineering course, student pairs run the direct shear test in soil mechanics after common instruction on shear-strength theory and the apparatus. During the assessed stages (running the experiment, processing raw data and calculating strength parameters, and writing individual lab reports with interpretation), pairs may consult freely available generative AI chatbots on their own devices for procedure, calculations, report structure and error analysis, while the teaching team intervenes only on safety or equipment grounds. Assessment combines a team operation score, an individual report and a team presentation defended under peer questioning. The authors report higher scores for the AI-assisted group, and also document overreliance, including uncritical acceptance of generated output and alteration of discrepant data without adequate verification; the source notes no instructor-led verification of AI output was provided.
acts.t: Generative AI as a consultable lab partner in a soil mechanics direct shear test, with a defended presentation

srp: To develop graduate science and engineering students' knowledge of AI ethics and their awareness and problem-solving in relation to ethical dilemmas in AI development and use.

Within a mandatory online Ethics of Research course, students complete an approximately five-hour AI ethics module, choose from seven real-world case studies, reflect explicitly on ethical considerations and potential solutions, and complete pre- and post-intervention knowledge, awareness and open-response measures.

acts.sum: Inside a mandatory online research-ethics course that graduate science and engineering students take before submitting a research proposal, a module of about five hours addresses the ethics of AI. Students choose among seven real-world case studies of ethical dilemmas in AI development and use, such as autonomous vehicles, misuse of personal data from a dating website, and AI-generated art imitating well-known artists. For the chosen case they analyze the dilemma, reflect explicitly on the ethical considerations involved and propose possible solutions, drawing on international guidance including the OECD Recommendation on AI and IEEE reports. No AI tool is used; AI systems and their documented uses are the subject matter. The study measured knowledge, perceived awareness and open responses to a photograph prompt before and after the module.
acts.t: Case-based, explicit-reflective AI ethics module for graduate science and engineering students

acts.sum: For students who already know a topic, the roles are reversed: a chatbot plays a student who has studied the topic, and the student plays teacher. The student chooses what the chatbot should explain and how it should apply the concept, for example through a scene from a TV show, a poem or a short story. The chatbot writes a one-paragraph explanation and two applications, then asks how well it did. The student assesses the explanation and applications, names gaps and inconsistencies, including how the chatbot adapts the concept to new scenarios, and explains the corrections back to it; where the chatbot is right, the student explains how it illustrated the concept. Explaining forces the student to organize what they know and separates familiarity from fluency.
acts.t: Teaching the chatbot: students correct the model's explanation to expose gaps in their own fluency

acts.sum: Students write a short in-class essay on a topic they already know, using only human-generated sources and distraction-free tools. They then prompt a chatbot on the same topic to brainstorm research questions, simplify texts, map a research plan or suggest sources, documenting each step and how it affected their thinking. They evaluate their essay twice, once with a rubric co-created with the chatbot and once with personal or peer criteria, weighing the AI rubric's limits. A Socratic dialogue follows in which they press the chatbot with 'why', 'how' and 'what if' through three to five layers. They have the chatbot revise the original essay, write another human-only draft, ask a classmate and the chatbot to compare versions for rhetoric and voice, produce a final revision in their own voice, and answer reflection questions on authorship.

acts.sum: Students write broad, open-ended interview questions for a fictional or historical character that show understanding of the literary or historical context, refining them with a rubric and with peer and teacher feedback, and are taught journalistic thinking and to imagine what will get the character talking. They then interview the character using an AI tool of their choice, guided by an active-listening rubric, and may use voice chat where available. They share the transcript with the teacher for assessment of critical thinking, active listening and problem-solving. Finally they analyze the chatbot: whether it furthered their understanding and whether it mimicked the character as found in the book or history or missed characteristic nuances, and write a paper arguing their case with quoted transcript evidence compared against the book or textbook.

They paste in a feedback prompt developed on the Peer & AI Review + Reflection (PAIRR) project, which asks the chatbot to describe two strengths and two possible areas for revision with quotations from the draft, and add the draft and, optionally, the assignment instructions and rubric. They then treat the first response as the start of a conversation: pushing back on comments that seem wrong, asking for clarification, requesting a different version of the feedback, raising what it did not address, exploring what they are unsure about, and asking for writing strategies. acts.sum: Addressed to students who may be accused of using AI when they did not, the chapter explains that wrongful accusations can follow from an instructor's intuition about style or from detection software, whose vendors concede false positives and which researchers suspect may be biased against English language learners and neurodiverse students. It gives a procedure: keep a record of the writing process through Google Docs or Word version history or an extension that reports time spent and copy-pastes and can replay the text's evolution, even when installed after the fact; check any such tool's privacy policy for AI training or data sale and change default settings; or screen-record while writing, or record yourself when using speech recognition. Students double-check the instructor's guidance on allowed AI use, document and disclose any use, and know their rights to appeal and to show their work.
acts.t: Documenting the writing process as evidence against a false AI-use accusation

acts.sum: Within a large project broken into smaller components with repeated chances for feedback and revision, and with grading weighted toward process rather than the finished work, students begin with low-stakes free-writing such as brainstorming, without AI. They then use a chatbot to explore possible areas for further investigation based on the ideas their own exploratory writing produced, rather than asking it to generate ideas from nothing. Finally they critique the AI-suggested areas and revise them into an outline. The guide places this among thinking steps, such as brainstorming, formulating a position or outlining a solution, where allowing AI might help students' process, and says instructors may assess learning better at these stages than from finished work.
