srp: To design a high-accuracy workflow that reduces reviewer workload by using a large language model to screen titles and abstracts, and to develop optimal prompts for that review.

Human-screened records are split into development batches and a reserved test set; each PICO and exclusion criterion is written as a Boolean prompt field; prompts are refined on 50-record sets until all relevant records are found; final prompts are run on the test set and on two later review updates, and performance statistics are calculated.

acts.sum: A systematic-review team builds and validates prompts so that GPT-4o can screen titles and abstracts for a living review. Human screening decisions already made for the review serve as the reference standard. Records are split into a development set, drawn in batches, and a reserved test set, and two later review updates are held back for validation. Each PICO eligibility element and each exclusion criterion becomes a Boolean prompt field that the model answers TRUE or FALSE, with exclusion criteria tested first. Prompts are refined fifty records at a time until every relevant record is identified or further changes stop helping. The final prompts are then run on the test set and the validation updates, and sensitivity, specificity, accuracy and workload reduction are calculated. Very short or missing abstracts are flagged for manual review.
acts.t: Iterative PICO-derived prompt development for LLM title/abstract screening, with held-out test and validation sets
acts.tool: GPT-4o; EPPI Reviewer; OpenAI API via Azure

srp: To understand whether variability in model outputs affects screening accuracy, and to what extent, before relying on the prompts in future review updates.

The team selects 50 random records, submits the final prompts for that same set ten times, counts agreements with human screeners and divides by the number of runs, and interprets the percentage against published bands, reporting overall and per-criterion consistency.
A consistency percentage for the overall decision and individual exclusion criteria, and a judgment on whether stability is adequate.
Agreement with human screeners across repeated runs, interpreted against published accuracy bands.
acts.sum: Because a language model can give different answers to the same input, a systematic-review team checks how stable its final screening prompts are before relying on them in later updates. Fifty records are selected at random and submitted to the final prompts ten times. For each run the team counts how often the model's decision agrees with the human screeners and divides agreements by the number of runs to get a consistency percentage, reported separately for the overall include-or-exclude decision and for each exclusion criterion. The percentage is read against published bands, with 80 to 95 percent treated as on par with human reviewers, 60 to 80 percent as near par, and below 60 percent as subpar. The team then judges whether stability is adequate for the review and for which criteria it is not.
acts.t: Reliability audit of AI screening prompts by repeated runs on the same records

acts.sum: Before using a generative AI tool on research data, a researcher classifies the data as public, protected or highly protected and reads a permission matrix that crosses those classes with three deployment types: locally run models, enterprise models and public models. Public data may go to all three; protected data only to local or enterprise models; highly protected data is conditional on a local model and not permitted elsewhere. The researcher then checks the governing policies, namely their own institution's endorsed-tools list, the research funder's rules (including a prohibition on reviewers putting grant applications into AI systems) and the target journal's AI policy, and weighs the trade-off between control at the local end and performance at the public end. srp: Keep scientific content, interpretations and conclusions originating from and validated by the researcher, while allowing AI to improve clarity and flow after the drafting and revising are done.

acts.sum: For manuscripts and proposals the trainee writes the entire first draft alone, using a tool only for spelling and grammar. They then get feedback from the mentor and anyone else involved and revise by hand, and complete at least two such rounds. Only then may they ask AI to critique the text, suggest alternative phrasing, and point to specific places to revise for clarity and flow. The trainee makes the changes, reads closely, checks every claim and citation against its source, and takes full accountability. The guide lists what expertise is needed to catch: hallucinated or misrepresented citations, confidently incorrect scientific claims, inappropriate statistical interpretation and missing caveats. It pairs acceptable prompts, such as asking for a critique of a Methods paragraph's clarity and completeness, with unacceptable ones, such as expanding bullet points into a Discussion with citations or drafting an abstract from the introduction.
acts.t: Two rounds of human-only revision before AI may critique a manuscript or proposal

acts.sum: Rather than adopting the guide wholesale, a faculty member, program director or committee adapts it in seven steps. They identify the local context (program type, discipline norms, training stage, culture); calibrate the mastery threshold on which AI permission depends, keeping it functional, meaning the trainee can do the task, explain the reasoning and catch their own errors, rather than a fixed count of attempts; add discipline-specific tasks, examples and tooling to each task category; and choose an enforcement level (strict lab policy, strong program guidance, or institution-wide educational resource, or the recommended hybrid). srp: Reduce the manual burden of writing a data management plan while keeping the researcher as the authority over the document.

A researcher supplies an uploaded science write-up or a description of study design; an LLM-based generator returns a funder-format DMP draft; a Jupyter notebook scores the response against a sample document with SBERT similarity and ROUGE-L recall, comparing Llama 3.3-70b and GPT-4.1; human review comparing AI and human plans is a stated next step.

acts.sum: Research data management staff at a university curation center explore whether an LLM can take on the manual burden of writing data management plans. A researcher applying for a grant supplies a simple input, either an uploaded science write-up or a short description of the study design, and the generator returns a draft in the funder's format. The team evaluates drafts in a Jupyter notebook that sends the prompt and scores the response against a sample plan with SBERT semantic similarity and ROUGE-L recall, comparing Llama 3.3-70b and GPT-4.1 on a workstation with two 24 GB GPUs. The slides set out both the case for the tool (much standardized information and policy guidance, much manual entry) and the case against (researchers may accept output without scrutiny, some information is not standardized), and list human review of AI versus human plans as a next step.
acts.t: LLM-drafted funder data management plans from minimal researcher input, scored against a reference plan

acts.sum: When a dataset is deposited, curation staff first run mechanical validation with Frictionless Data, which produces technical findings such as a large number of missing cells in one row across named columns. They pass that report to an LLM and ask for a restatement a researcher can act on, for example that the data were not exported correctly and were cut off at that row. They also ask for advice beyond the linter: clearer column names where a label such as ID is ambiguous, ISO date-time formatting, and a draft data dictionary based on the probable field of science. The model is also used to fill a README template for the deposit. Staff treat all of this as a draft to check and verify, since the model may remove every abbreviation, suggest unnecessary changes or be confidently wrong, and domain-expert curators write reusable natural-language templates for their fields.

srp: Convert messy user-submitted registry requests into clean, structured and correct JSON records efficiently, without removing the curation team's review.

Requests are reviewed for scope and correctness and out-of-scope requests are closed with an explanation. For in-scope requests an LLM adds language tags, reformats fields and removes placeholder text in new records, and converts free-text change descriptions into the update encoding syntax for updates. Metadata is reviewed automatically and manually, release preparation runs duplication and integrity checks, and the release is published; the process runs in a GitHub workflow.
Clean, consistent JSON records and encoded update instructions ready for curator review, release checks and publication to the registry API and data dump.
Automatic and manual metadata review, then data-duplication and integrity checks before release.
acts.sum: Registry curators who receive messy, user-submitted requests to add or update organization records insert a large language model call at two points in an existing review-and-release workflow. For a new record, the model adds language tags to name metadata, reformats field inputs so they are clean and consistent, and strips placeholder text; for an update, it converts the requester's free-text description of the change into the registry's formal update syntax. The curation team still decides whether each request is in scope and correct, reviews prepared metadata both automatically and manually, and runs duplication and integrity checks before a release is published to the API and data dump. Out-of-scope or incorrect requests are closed with an explanation. The workflow runs inside a version-controlled GitHub process, and the output is structured JSON ready for curator review.
acts.t: LLM structuring of free-text registry submissions into reviewable records within a curation workflow

srp: To test how far open-source generative models can approximate thematic-analysis steps so researchers can inductively build codebooks from very large corpora without redundant codes.

Each text unit is summarized into atomic points in light of the research questions; points are embedded, reduced and clustered; for each cluster the nearest existing codes are retrieved and the model decides whether a new code and definition are needed; generated codes are then clustered and themes identified, with temperature at zero and the code-creation rate tracked.

acts.sum: A qualitative researcher facing more open-ended responses than a team could read builds an inductive codebook with the GATOS workflow, run on open-weight models so the data can stay under the researcher's control. Each response is summarized into atomic summary points framed by the researcher's stated research questions. The points are embedded, reduced in dimensionality and clustered. For each cluster, the nearest existing codes are retrieved and the model decides whether they already cover the cluster or whether a new code and definition are needed. Finally the codes are clustered and a model names themes. Temperature is set to zero, and the rate of new-code creation across clusters is tracked as a check that redundancy control is working. The researcher frames the questions, can seed their own codes, and evaluates the resulting codebook before applying it.
acts.t: GATOS: six-step inductive codebook generation with open-weight models and a retrieval-checked new-code decision

acts.sum: To test a new qualitative coding method against a known answer, a research team generates synthetic open-ended responses with themes deliberately planted in them, borrowing the logic of simulation studies in quantitative methods. An open-source model generates personas, several imaginary contexts per dataset, and eight themes with eight sub-themes each; the researchers themselves specify data type, collection context, writing style and length, and choose generation models for their permissive licenses. A fixed number of responses is sampled per sub-theme rather than the full combinatorial space. Output is requested in JSON so that a parsing failure flags a failure to follow instructions, and those cases are inspected and discarded. Team members review the responses for realism against responses seen in prior studies and record which criteria were model-generated and which researcher-specified.

Thirty-seven single-proposition questions were grouped into nine blocks, run through the synthesis engine on a stated date and exported separately in RIS; records and DOI-unique records were counted; for two questions on young, unevenly indexed literature, field-tagged searches were run in a bibliographic database as a second channel and the divergence reported.

acts.sum: A researcher building an evidence base for an argument writes claim-level questions, each stating a single empirically answerable proposition, and groups them into thematic blocks keyed to the argument before any retrieval. Each question runs through an AI evidence-synthesis engine on a recorded date, and each result, with its consensus indication, screening account, findings, limitations and reference list, is exported separately in a reference-manager format. The researcher counts records and identifier-unique records, treats round-number set sizes as export ceilings rather than corpus sizes, and identifies questions whose literature is young, unevenly indexed or preprint-heavy. For those, field-tagged searches built with a general assistant are run in a bibliographic database as a second, independent channel, and the divergence between channels is reported as a measurement. Anomalies such as conflated literatures are recorded.
acts.t: Claim-level AI evidence synthesis with a second independent retrieval channel and dated counts

acts.sum: An AI-assisted synthesis produces candidate references and figures, and this gate decides what may enter a draft. No author string, year, volume or page range is typed from a model's output; each is transcribed only from an identifier-matched record exported by a reference manager. The identifier serves as the match key because titles and identifiers are the elements most likely to be reproduced correctly, whereas authorship and pagination are where discrepancies appear. The researcher picks the load-bearing figures in the argument, traces at least one to the study that made the measurement rather than to the source that reported it, and keeps a verification log documenting at least one catch, such as a substituted author string or a figure attributed to a synthesis. Where the primary source cannot be obtained, the figure is explicitly downgraded to the citing author's summary.

srp: Determine whether generative AI can support expert-led research data governance without undermining quality, accountability or trust, by supporting rather than replacing professional judgment in plan review.

Experts configure criteria derived from national evaluation guidance; the tool evaluates each question, traces judgments to sentences in the plan and flags uncertainty; experts review flagged questions, form the assessment and author feedback, while anonymized notes and statistics feed back into the criteria.

acts.sum: Data management experts in a university library who review researchers' data management plans configure a set of evaluation criteria, structured as sections, topics and questions derived from national funder guidance, each with a normative level, applicability condition and guidance. The tool evaluates an uploaded plan question by question, returning a yes, partial or no label with the plan sentences it relied on, and reports compliance, disagreement and uncertainty, separating ambiguous criteria, failed retrieval and inconsistent inference. The expert reads each judgment against the traced sentences, concentrates on the questions flagged as uncertain, forms the final assessment and writes the feedback to the researcher. Sensitive text can be anonymized locally before processing, and anonymized notes and statistics are kept to refine the criteria over time.
acts.t: AI-supported expert review of data management plans with configurable criteria, uncertainty flagging and a sentence-level audit trail

acts.sum: Before adopting an AI tool that evaluates data management plans, data management experts at two university libraries run a validation. They evaluate a set of plans with the tool (28 in the source, producing 556 expert labels at about 50 minutes per plan), record their own labels against its judgments, and sort the criteria questions into five complexity categories, from explicit check to adequacy judgment. For each category they compute consistency across repeated runs and models and the rate of expert-AI agreement, compare results between the two sites, and catalog failure modes such as keyword-literal matching of criteria, false negatives on non-relevant questions, claims that a regulation was mentioned when it was not, and template text being evaluated. Each challenge is mapped to a development action, and the experts note that reviewing only flagged questions limits how the results can be read.
acts.t: Expert validation audit of an AI assessment tool using question-complexity categories, consistency and agreement rates

acts.sum: Staff responsible for institutional AI literacy design a program stratified by responsibility rather than one course for everyone. All students complete a short orientation early and before any assessed work where AI may matter, with completion recorded; all staff complete a longer core course; assessment designers, tool approvers and procurers, and staff handling student data receive role-specific training; and senior leaders get a briefing on oversight, risk appetite and escalation. Content spans types of AI, how generative models produce fluent but sometimes inaccurate output, and ethical application, taught through a curated repository of real documented failures. An Academic Owner and a Service Owner are named under senior oversight, student ambassadors co-design and deliver peer sessions, and training is kept short, accessible, on demand, refreshed after major changes, tied to actual policy processes, and tracked through completion records and a change-log.
acts.t: Designing a stratified institutional AI literacy program with role-specific tiers and named owners

acts.sum: After core training sets a shared baseline, each faculty or school interprets institutional AI principles through its own standards of evidence and teaching practice and produces a small number of concrete exemplars within an initial adoption period. The minimum set is an assessment brief that states clearly what AI use is permitted, a worked evaluation of AI-generated material against the discipline's standards of evidence, and an identification of ethical, accessibility or bias concerns specific to the field. The source's examples include marking where generative tools can support preparatory work in the humanities without displacing interpretive labor, showing legitimate data-handling or coding uses in the sciences while stating that manipulating results remains misconduct, and addressing regulatory obligations in accredited professional programs. Exemplars are shared institution-wide for other programs to adapt and revisited as tools change.

acts.sum: Before any market contact for a generative AI tool used in teaching, including vendor demonstrations where institutional data or materials might be shared, the proposing unit writes a public value case. It states the educational purpose as a problem tied to learning outcomes or teaching quality, with expected benefits and a plan to evaluate them; records the non-AI alternatives considered, such as pedagogic redesign, staffing, peer support or existing tools, and why AI is preferred; states the institution's risk appetite, including what will not be accepted, for example automated grading without robust oversight; identifies stakeholders; and scopes the regulatory classification and any high-risk triggers. Nothing proceeds until procurement and a registrar-level Policy Owner accept the case. Named role-holders then review minimum vendor evidence on security posture, breach response, change management with release notes, and independent verification, and student representatives are consulted on material changes.
acts.t: Pre-procurement public value case and minimum vendor evidence review for a generative AI tool

acts.sum: A one-page deposited prompt turns a general chatbot into a coaching-style mentor for faculty facing a mentoring or research-team management problem, framed as a confidential space to practice difficult, high-stakes conversations. The prompt gives the model the persona of a tenured full professor grounded in evidence-based mentorship practice (National Academies, CIMER), whose goal is to help the user reach their own solution. You paste the prompt into a new chat and describe the problem. The model then acknowledges the difficulty and asks one clarifying question, asks you to see the situation from the student's side or from six months ahead, and asks for one concrete step you could take this week before offering two or three suggestions built on your idea. It closes with a long-view perspective and stops.

acts.sum: Participants use a four-level reflective frame to examine how they use generative AI rather than whether they use it. For each of ten human purposes (explore, understand, evaluate, create, plan, rehearse, regulate, curate, reflect, connect) they name the concrete activities they hand to AI, identify the human capabilities in play that the use could strengthen or erode, and answer a reflective question about their own practice, such as whether they still decide what is worth pursuing when AI generates possibilities. An educator introduces the frame as a prompt for honest conversation rather than a score or checklist, works through the domains most relevant to the group, and closes with three global questions about AI's greatest contribution, the participant's greatest concern, and the capabilities they want to keep developing. No AI tool is used during the activity; the output is a written reflective account.
acts.t: Four-level reflective frame mapping AI use against the human capabilities it strengthens or erodes

acts.sum: A self-reflection profile accompanies the reflective frame. The participant rates each of ten human purposes for AI use on four one-to-five scales: Use (how often they use AI there), Confidence (how confident they feel using it), Development (how much they want to develop in that area), and Agency (how confident they are that their own judgment remains active). acts.sum: A community college library and its student engagement office convened thirteen students as a workgroup for one quarter to write the college's first academic use policy for generative AI. Instead of a blank page, the students worked from a published kit: a critical review of AI policies in higher education assessment, a policy evaluation tool, a selection of faculty course-level AI policies, a self-checklist, policy writing guidelines from another university and a policy proposal rubric from a third, plus examples of student-written policies elsewhere. srp: Help institutions understand how the regulation applies to teaching and assessment, identify heightened exposure, and treat compliance as an ongoing process.

Examine the system's actual function; test it against five high-risk educational uses; classify as consequential or learning support and apply the corresponding obligations; record purpose, non-purposes and safeguards; reassess when a pilot enters routine teaching; require vendor statements on emotion inference; review analytics; carry disclosures in syllabi and briefs.

acts.sum: Academic and governance staff examine what a candidate or in-use AI system actually does in teaching, looking past its label and marketing, and test that function against five educational uses the EU AI Act designates high risk: admission decisions, grading that affects progression or certification, determining learning pathways, monitoring behavior during assessment, and eligibility for support. They classify the use as consequential decision-making, which requires documentation, oversight and accountability, or as learning support, which requires transparency and proportionate governance, and record what the tool is for, what it is not for and what safeguards apply. They set a trigger to reassess when a pilot moves into routine or credit-bearing teaching, require vendors to state plainly whether a system infers emotion, review classroom analytics against prohibited practices, and carry the resulting disclosures into syllabi and assessment briefs.
acts.t: Classifying an AI system in teaching and learning by function against high-risk regulatory triggers

srp: Ensure generative AI adoption does not reinforce or amplify existing and intersectional disadvantage, and that commitments to inclusion become measurable action.

Apply explicit equity criteria in procurement and approval; defer approval where transparency or reliability cannot be demonstrated; check licensing and infrastructure for equitable access; evaluate language performance; adopt approved tools or require declarations for assessment; run regular equity audits reporting disaggregated outcomes, with redress pathways and student representation.

acts.sum: Governance, procurement and academic staff build equity into institutional AI adoption at approval and afterward. At approval they apply explicit equity criteria, asking for evidence of representative training data and of the vendor's awareness of system limitations, and defer approval where transparency or reliability cannot be shown until identified risks are mitigated. They check that licensing and infrastructure, including broadband and hardware, give equitable access across disciplines and to individual learners who might otherwise be excluded, and evaluate systems for performance in the relevant minority or additional language, arranging supports or alternatives where it falls short. For assessment they choose between approved tools and declarations for private systems. They then run regular equity audits that report disaggregated outcomes, maintain complaint and redress pathways, and place students in AI governance.
acts.t: Equity audit and precautionary approval for institutional AI adoption, with disaggregated outcome reporting

Conduct environmental impact assessments; seek vendor energy disclosure; prefer low-energy models with comparable outcomes; include energy and carbon transparency in procurement; monitor and audit energy use; share findings; write open standards, portability and exit strategies into procurement; review dependencies periodically.
Per-system impact assessments, vendor disclosures, procurement terms, regular energy audits and periodic dependency reviews with exit strategies.
acts.sum: Procurement, sustainability and academic governance staff build environmental and resilience checks into AI adoption. For each proposed system they carry out an environmental impact assessment, ask the vendor to disclose energy use and sustainability measures, prefer efficient, lower-energy models where educational outcomes are comparable, and write energy sourcing and carbon commitments into procurement documentation. After adoption they monitor environmental impact and run regular audits of AI-related energy consumption, turning findings into action and sharing them across the sector where possible. A resilience strand designs the AI ecosystem to avoid dependence on a single platform or vendor, writes open standards, data portability and exit strategies into procurement, and periodically reviews dependencies for points of failure, weighing environmental, educational and financial sustainability together.
acts.t: Environmental and resilience review of institutional AI adoption, with energy audits and exit strategies

srp: Give an institution a proportionate, integrated way of reflecting on how its generative AI practice aligns with the framework, and turn reflection into sector learning.

Develop reflection mechanisms within existing governance and quality arrangements; address five named dimensions; review regularly; share summaries with staff, students and the wider academic community.
A reflective account across five dimensions and a summary shared with staff, students and the sector.
acts.sum: Quality assurance and academic governance staff build a proportionate reflection on the institution's generative AI practice into existing governance and quality arrangements rather than a parallel process. They compile an account addressing five dimensions: strategic decisions on AI in teaching, learning and assessment; developments in assessment design and academic integrity; staff development and capacity-building for AI literacy and pedagogical adaptation; ethical, operational or integrity concerns that arose and how they were addressed; and planning and investment decisions for responsible and sustainable adoption. The review recurs regularly because the technology changes quickly, and a summary of the reflection is shared with staff, students and the wider academic community. No AI tool is used; the output is a written account and a public summary.
acts.t: Institutional reflective account of generative AI practice on five dimensions, shared for sector learning
